client: I've been really struggling since my partner passed away from cancer six months ago. Everything just feels empty now, and I can't seem to enjoy anything like I used to. My friends keep inviting me out, but I just feel like a burden when I'm with them - like I'm bringing the whole mood down with my grief.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying such a heavy weight of grief, and that emptiness you describe is completely understandable after such a profound loss. I notice you mention feeling like a burden to your friends - could you tell me more about what specifically makes you feel that way when you're with them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know...I guess it's because they always look so uncomfortable when I start talking about how sad I am. Like they don't know what to say, so they quickly change the subject. It makes me feel like my grief is something they just want to avoid dealing with.
therapist: The pain in your voice is palpable when you describe how your friends respond to your grief. It sounds like their discomfort leaves you feeling even more alone in your sorrow. Have you considered what kind of support from them might feel more helpful to you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know what would actually help from them, that's the problem. When they try to say comforting things like "he's in a better place" or "time heals all wounds," it just makes me feel worse because it feels so empty. But then when they avoid talking about it altogether, that hurts too because it's like my pain doesn't matter. I feel like I can't win either way.
therapist: You're caught in such a painful dilemma - wanting understanding but finding that neither words of comfort nor silence truly meet your needs. This raw, honest expression of how isolated you feel in your grief is an important step - would it help to explore what kind of responses from friends might actually feel meaningful to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess I just don't know what would help anymore. When friends try to comfort me with platitudes like "they're in a better place," it feels empty, but when they say nothing at all, that hurts too. Maybe I'm being unfair, but nothing seems to land right when I'm feeling this alone.
therapist: Your frustration comes through so clearly - it must feel like no response from your friends can possibly match the depth of what you're experiencing. That sense of loneliness when others' attempts at comfort fall short is incredibly painful - would you be willing to share what a truly supportive response might look like to you in this moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Honestly, I don't even know what a supportive response would look like anymore. When people try to comfort me, it just feels... performative, like they're going through the motions. Maybe if someone actually sat with me in the discomfort instead of rushing to fix it - but I don't know if that would help either. I'm just stuck in this cycle where every attempt at connection makes me feel more alone.
therapist: Your words carry such deep exhaustion with the way people try to comfort you - that sense of performative support must make the loneliness even more isolating. The way you describe wanting someone to just sit with you in the discomfort rather than trying to fix it suggests you're craving genuine presence more than solutions right now. Would you be willing to explore what that kind of presence might look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client:
It's like you actually get it - that's such a relief to hear. But at the same time, I don't even know what genuine presence would look like anymore. When people try to be there for me, I just end up feeling guilty for burdening them with my problems. 

The idea of exploring this makes me anxious because what if we figure out what I need and I still can't get it? That might hurt even more than just being lonely now.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling caught between hope and fear - relieved to feel understood, yet worried that exploring your needs might lead to more disappointment. That sense of guilt you describe about burdening others seems to be adding another layer to your pain. Would it be helpful to unpack where that feeling of being a burden might be coming from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, that’s exactly how it feels—like I’m stuck between hoping things can change and fearing they won’t. I do feel like a burden a lot of the time, especially when I try to open up to friends or family. It’s like I’m always second-guessing myself, wondering if I’m being too much or if they’re just humoring me. I guess part of it comes from growing up, where expressing needs wasn’t really encouraged, but it’s hard to shake that feeling now.
therapist: It sounds like this pattern of second-guessing yourself runs deep, rooted in those early experiences where expressing needs wasn't safe. That hesitation you feel now - wondering if you're "too much" - makes so much sense given that history. Would you be open to exploring how these old patterns might be shaping your expectations of how others will respond to you now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think you're right that it stems from my childhood, but I'm not sure how much exploring it will help. I mean, I can’t change the past, and I don’t want to keep blaming everything on it. I just feel stuck because I still worry about being "too much" whenever I try to speak up or ask for what I need. It’s exhausting to always second-guess myself.
therapist: I hear both determination and weariness in your voice - you want to move forward without getting stuck in the past, yet that fear of being "too much" continues to weigh heavily on you. What would it feel like to experiment with small steps toward trusting that your needs matter, even with this understandable hesitation you carry?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I want to believe my needs matter, but it's so hard when past experiences keep proving the opposite. Every time I've tried to speak up or ask for what I need, I've been dismissed or made to feel like a burden. Even thinking about small steps makes me anxious - what if people pull away again?
therapist: The pain in your voice is so clear when you describe how past rejections make it hard to hope for something different now. That anxiety about people pulling away again makes complete sense given what you've been through - would it help to explore what support might look like that wouldn't feel like such a risk to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly, I’m not sure what kind of support wouldn’t feel risky. Every time I’ve tried to open up or rely on someone, it’s ended badly. I just feel like I’m setting myself up for disappointment again. It’s hard to imagine anything different when the pattern keeps repeating.
therapist: Your weariness comes through so clearly - it makes complete sense that you'd feel hesitant to hope for something different when past experiences have taught you that opening up leads to disappointment. That fear of setting yourself up for more hurt is completely understandable. Would it feel safer to start by exploring what support might look like in very small, controlled ways?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
